nodes.name: Sal
nodes.desc: The dominant tree of the moist deciduous forest that covers most of the reserve. Wikipedia notes sal regenerates poorly here while other trees come up well.

nodes.name: Tall riverside grasses
nodes.desc: Grasslands cover roughly a tenth of the reserve, mostly along the river valleys, and feed the deer and elephants that graze there.

nodes.name: Fig trees
nodes.desc: Fruiting trees of the forest edge and riverbanks. Their fruit is food for monkeys, langurs, birds and deer.

nodes.name: River algae
nodes.desc: Green films on stones in the Ramganga and its reservoir that feed fish.

nodes.name: Chital
nodes.desc: The most commonly recorded deer near the reserve and a staple prey of its tigers and leopards.

nodes.name: Sambar
nodes.desc: A large forest deer that browses leaves and grazes; adults are a main prey of tigers.

nodes.name: Hog deer
nodes.desc: A small grassland deer of the river plains. Wikipedia notes its numbers fell sharply after the Kalagarh dam flooded riverside habitat.

nodes.name: Asian elephant
nodes.desc: A grazing and browsing giant that can eat up to about 150 kg of plants a day. Tigers sometimes take calves.

nodes.name: Tarai gray langur
nodes.desc: A leaf and fruit eating monkey of the forest and its edges, hunted by leopards and tigers.

nodes.name: Red junglefowl
nodes.desc: A ground-feeding forest bird, the wild ancestor of the chicken, and prey for cats and snakes.

nodes.name: Golden mahseer
nodes.desc: A large river fish of Himalayan rivers that grazes algae and other foods and feeds the gharial.

nodes.name: Oriental rat snake
nodes.desc: A fast ground snake of forest and fields that eats small vertebrates and is itself prey of the king cobra.

nodes.name: King cobra
nodes.desc: Mainly eats other snakes and lizards, and lives in the Himalayan foothills including the Terai.

nodes.name: Golden jackal
nodes.desc: A flexible hunter and scavenger, and GloBI records show it feeding on chital and sambar.

nodes.name: Large-billed crow
nodes.desc: An opportunistic bird that feeds at carcasses; one GloBI record shows it eating chital.

nodes.name: Gharial
nodes.desc: A fish-eating crocodilian released into the Ramganga from the late 1970s. A 2015 survey counted 90 animals, many near the reservoir shore.

nodes.name: Indian leopard
nodes.desc: A smaller cat than the tiger that takes deer, langurs and jackals, and sometimes is killed by tigers.

nodes.name: Bengal tiger
nodes.desc: The reserve flagship, hunting chital, sambar, hog deer and langurs; Wikipedia reports 260 tigers counted in 2022.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Drives growth in the dense sal canopy and on the open river grasslands.

nodes.name: Monsoon rain
nodes.desc: Summer monsoon rains feed the rivers and the lush forest growth.

nodes.name: Ramganga and reservoir
nodes.desc: The Ramganga runs through the reserve and the Kalagarh dam flooded about 80 km2 of riverine land, creating habitat for fish and gharial.

nodes.name: Leaf litter and alluvial soil
nodes.desc: Forest floor and river deposits where nutrients are recycled for trees and grasses.

nodes.name: Fungi, termites & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down leaf litter, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
